C01.text:
# Decision and information boundaries

Winning objective, legal joint choices, disclosed information, and the distinction between observations and hypotheses.

## Reference text

Select a supplied legal joint action for the current request. In an ordinary doubles move request, a joint action specifies what both active Pokémon will do, including any selected targets, switches, and permitted Mega Evolution declaration. Evaluate how the two actions work together.

The objective is to improve the chance of winning the whole battle. Immediate damage is one consideration alongside survival, removing threats, protecting a partner, controlling action order, preserving useful reserves, creating favorable positions, and managing limited resources. These are decision objectives, not additional battle mechanics.

Treat the supplied current observation as the factual description of this decision point. Distinguish confirmed information, explicitly supplied open-set information, estimates, and hypotheses. A common opponent set is not a confirmed set. A possible opponent response is not its announced action. An unknown item is different from a confirmed absence of an item.

Use the supplied Champions-specific definitions. Do not fill a gap by silently borrowing a value from another Pokémon game. A species can have a different form, current type, ability, or effective statistics from its usual starting form. Current battle transformations and revealed effects matter.

Only supplied candidates can be selected. A candidate's inclusion means it can be submitted under the information available when the list was assembled; it does not guarantee that the move will hit, that its effect will succeed, or that no newly revealed restriction will invalidate it. An attack into an immunity can still be a selectable action.

C02.text:
# Requests and simultaneous commands

Simultaneous commands, move requests, team selection, and replacement decisions within a turn.

## Reference text

Both players normally choose commands before seeing the opponent's commands for that turn. The commands then execute in the battle's action order. A Pokémon usually has one chosen action in a turn; an effect can explicitly alter, repeat, cancel, or replace an action.

A request may instead ask for team selection, a forced replacement, or a replacement after a pivot move. Such a request is a separate decision point and may occur during an unfinished turn. A Pokémon entering through a replacement does not inherit the departing Pokémon's unexecuted ordinary attack.

The state and candidate list belong to one request. Previously selected actions, targets, and available switches can become stale after a knockout, switch, revealed restriction, or other state change. A fresh request needs a fresh decision from its supplied options.

C03.text:
# Action order

Priority brackets, effective Speed, ties, dynamic ordering, switches, and Mega Evolution timing.

## Reference text

For ordinary actions in this environment, voluntary switches execute before Mega Evolution, and Mega Evolution executes before ordinary moves. Entry effects caused by those switches can change the field before the attacks occur. Explicit preparation effects and interrupting events have their own timing.

Move priority is considered before Speed. A higher priority bracket acts before a lower one regardless of the ordinary Speed comparison. Within the same priority bracket, faster Pokémon normally act first. Equal effective Speed can be resolved randomly. Specific effects can force a Pokémon earlier or later within an order bracket.

Some illustrative move priorities are:

| Move or family | Ordinary priority |
| --- | ---: |
| Helping Hand | +5 |
| Protect and Detect | +4 |
| Fake Out, Wide Guard, Quick Guard | +3 |
| Follow Me, Rage Powder, Feint, First Impression | +2 |
| Sucker Punch | +1 |
| Most attacks and many status moves | 0 |
| Roar and Dragon Tail | -6 |
| Trick Room | -7 |

These values do not replace the current definition of a move. Abilities or other effects can alter priority. For example, Prankster raises the priority of status moves. An effect that makes a Pokémon act early within its bracket does not necessarily give its move positive priority for Psychic Terrain or Quick Guard.

Speed is updated as the turn progresses. A Speed change, paralysis, Tailwind, weather-dependent Speed ability, Mega Evolution, or other applicable change can reorder actions that have not executed. A Pokémon that has already acted does not receive another ordinary action merely because Speed changes.

Trick Room reverses the Speed comparison within a priority bracket. It does not reverse priority brackets or make an ordinary negative-priority move precede a positive-priority move. Trick Room has no extreme-Speed wraparound in Champions.

C04.text:
# Move execution and failure

Execution checks, interrupted actions, PP expenditure, and events that change a move before it resolves.

## Reference text

When a Pokémon reaches its action, it must still be able to act. Sleep, freeze, flinching, confusion, paralysis, recharge, and move restrictions can prevent or alter execution. Their checks have different timings; do not assume all possible failure rolls occur independently on every turn.

Being unable to act before the move starts is different from using a move that misses or is blocked. The ordinary engine checks whether the Pokémon can move before deducting PP. A move that proceeds to execution normally spends PP even if it subsequently misses or fails, subject to its specific rules.

For an ordinary attack, relevant checks include whether the target can be reached, protection or interception effects, type immunity, move-specific immunity, accuracy, and the hit's damage and effects. Individual moves may add their own conditions. A move's listed secondary effect does not bypass those conditions merely because its listed chance is 100%.

Events caused by one action can resolve before the next Pokémon acts. These include item consumption, reactive abilities, stat changes, knockouts, and switches. A selected target or partner may therefore have changed by the time an action is executed.

C05.text:
# Targets and field positions

Target categories, positions, ally targeting, replacements, retargeting, and redirection.

## Reference text

The active field contains up to two Pokémon per side. In ordinary doubles, each active Pokémon is adjacent to the other three active positions. Use the supplied action's explicit target rather than inferring a target from the move's name.

| Target meaning | Interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| Self | The user. |
| Adjacent other Pokémon | A selected adjacent Pokémon other than the user; this may include an ally when permitted. |
| Adjacent foe | One selected adjacent opposing Pokémon. |
| Adjacent ally | The user's active partner. |
| Ally or self | A selected partner or the user. |
| All adjacent foes | All eligible opposing active positions. |
| All adjacent Pokémon | All eligible adjacent positions, including the user's partner, but not the user. |
| Ally side | An effect attached to the user's side. |
| Foe side | An effect attached to the opposing side. |
| Entire field | A field-wide effect, which follows its own rules. |
| Random target | The engine selects a target under the move's rules. |

Targets are generally resolved through positions. If the selected opponent switches, the replacement occupying that position ordinarily becomes the target. Ally Switch changes which Pokémon occupies each allied position without withdrawing either Pokémon.

If a selected opposing target has fainted before the action, an ordinary eligible single-target move can be redirected automatically to a remaining foe. A move specifically aimed at a fainted ally can fail instead. Automatic target selection does not turn an attack with no remaining foes into an attack against the user's partner. Special target-selection moves need their own definitions.

Redirection is an additional mechanic. Follow Me, Rage Powder, Lightning Rod, and Storm Drain can change a suitable single target. A move that hits multiple positions does not become a single-target move merely because only one Pokémon is presently affected. See the redirection and protection entries in the mechanics library.

C06.text:
# Spread moves and ally damage

Multiple targets, spread damage reduction, separate hit outcomes, protection, and ally exposure.

## Reference text

A move targeting all adjacent Pokémon can damage the user's partner. A move targeting all adjacent foes ordinarily does not hit that partner. Consider each target's type, ability, item, protection, and current condition separately.

For ordinary damaging spread moves, the damage modifier is 0.75 when the engine identifies more than one target. This is a per-target damage reduction, not a division of one fixed damage pool among the targets.

The engine marks the move as a spread hit before resolving individual targets' protection and immunity checks. Consequently, one target protecting or being immune does not necessarily restore full single-target damage against the other target. A move with only one initial target can avoid the spread penalty. Special multi-target or multi-hit moves can use different rules.

Accuracy and other target-specific outcomes can differ between targets. One opponent being hit does not prove the other will be hit. Wide Guard protection depends on the move's target category, not simply on how many Pokémon happen to take damage.

C07.text:
# Move properties

Move type, category, power, accuracy, target, contact, tags, secondary effects, and self effects.

## Reference text

Keep these concepts distinct:

- **Type** determines ordinary type effectiveness and same-type attack bonus.
- **Category** is Physical, Special, or Status. It is independent of type.
- **Base power** is an input to damage, not the resulting HP loss.
- **Accuracy** describes an ordinary hit check. A move that bypasses that check can still fail against protection, an immunity, or an unreachable target.
- **Priority** places the move in an action-order bracket.
- **Contact** is a separate property. Not all physical moves make contact, and contact is not determined by damage category.
- **Spread targeting** determines the set of targets; it is not synonymous with multiple hits.
- **Secondary effects** are effects handled after the relevant primary hit, such as a chance to flinch or lower a statistic. Some moves have important primary effects instead.
- **Self effects** affect the user, such as recoil or a Special Attack drop, and can have different conditions from effects on the target.
- **Move tags** such as sound, powder, bullet, pulse, punch, slicing, bite, wind, and healing matter when a supplied ability or item refers to them.

A Showdown `protect` flag means that the move is normally blockable by protection. It does not mean the move protects its user. A `bypasssub` flag concerns Substitute, not Protect. Keep these meanings separate.

C08.text:
# Complete ordinary type matchups

The complete ordinary matchup table for the eighteen types, dual-type multiplication, and explicit exceptions.

## Reference text

Read this table by **attacking move type**. Types in the second column receive 2× damage from that attack type; types in the third receive 0.5×; types in the fourth receive 0×. Every unlisted attacking/defending pair is 1×. This specifies all 324 ordinary matchups among the 18 types.

| Attacking type | 2× against | 0.5× against | 0× against |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Normal | — | Rock, Steel | Ghost |
| Fire | Grass, Ice, Bug, Steel | Fire, Water, Rock, Dragon | — |
| Water | Fire, Ground, Rock | Water, Grass, Dragon | — |
| Electric | Water, Flying | Electric, Grass, Dragon | Ground |
| Grass | Water, Ground, Rock | Fire, Grass, Poison, Flying, Bug, Dragon, Steel | — |
| Ice | Grass, Ground, Flying, Dragon | Fire, Water, Ice, Steel | — |
| Fighting | Normal, Ice, Rock, Dark, Steel | Poison, Flying, Psychic, Bug, Fairy | Ghost |
| Poison | Grass, Fairy | Poison, Ground, Rock, Ghost | Steel |
| Ground | Fire, Electric, Poison, Rock, Steel | Grass, Bug | Flying |
| Flying | Grass, Fighting, Bug | Electric, Rock, Steel | — |
| Psychic | Fighting, Poison | Psychic, Steel | Dark |
| Bug | Grass, Psychic, Dark | Fire, Fighting, Poison, Flying, Ghost, Steel, Fairy | — |
| Rock | Fire, Ice, Flying, Bug | Fighting, Ground, Steel | — |
| Ghost | Psychic, Ghost | Dark | Normal |
| Dragon | Dragon | Steel | Fairy |
| Dark | Psychic, Ghost | Fighting, Dark, Fairy | — |
| Steel | Ice, Rock, Fairy | Fire, Water, Electric, Steel | — |
| Fairy | Fighting, Dragon, Dark | Fire, Poison, Steel | — |

For a Pokémon with two current types, multiply the two ordinary modifiers. This can give 4×, 2×, 1×, 0.5×, 0.25×, or immunity. An immunity dominates the product unless a specific effect removes or bypasses it. A single type is applied once.

Use current defensive types. A Mega Evolution or a type-changing effect can alter the matchup before an attack. Type-specific exceptions such as Freeze-Dry, immunity-bypassing abilities, grounding, and move-specific effectiveness belong to the applicable entity definitions.

This table describes ordinary attack effectiveness. It is not a universal rule for whether a status move works. For example, type-based status immunity, powder immunity, and Prankster immunity are separate checks.

C09.text:
# Other type-based immunities

Type-based status, powder, trapping, Prankster, and weather immunities beyond ordinary damage effectiveness.

## Reference text

Under the ordinary rules, Fire types cannot newly receive burn; Electric types cannot newly receive paralysis; Ice types cannot newly receive freeze; and Poison and Steel types cannot newly receive poison or bad poison. Corrosion is a specific exception to the ordinary poisoning type restriction when applicable.

Grass types are immune to powder effects. This includes the relevant check for whether an attacker follows Rage Powder's redirection. Grass types are also immune to the initial application of Leech Seed through that move's specific rule.

Ghost types are immune to ordinary trapping restrictions. This does not mean they can ignore every move lock, charging turn, or other limitation. Opposing Dark types are immune to applicable status moves boosted by Prankster; this is not immunity to all status moves or all priority attacks.

Rock, Ground, and Steel types are immune to ordinary sandstorm chip damage. Only Rock types receive sandstorm's Special Defense increase. Ice types receive snow's Defense increase. Snow does not deal the old hail chip damage.

Changing into an immune type does not by itself mean an existing major status is cured. Apply any explicit cure or removal effect separately.

C10.text:
# Statistics and stat stages

Unboosted versus effective statistics, stat-stage multipliers, stage limits, and Champions stat-point conventions.

## Reference text

HP describes current and maximum health. Attack and Defense normally govern physical damage; Special Attack and Special Defense normally govern special damage. Speed governs ordinary order within a priority bracket. Accuracy and evasion are separate battle stages rather than ordinary trained statistics.

The supplied stat fields must distinguish species base stats, actual unboosted battle stats, stat stages, and any already modified effective stats. Do not apply the same modifier twice. If the input gives an actual stat plus a stage, the stage still matters; if it explicitly gives an effective value that already includes that stage, use that fact.

Ordinary Attack, Defense, Special Attack, Special Defense, and Speed stages range from -6 to +6:

| Stage | Multiplier |
| --- | ---: |
| -6 | 1/4 |
| -5 | 2/7 |
| -4 | 1/3 |
| -3 | 2/5 |
| -2 | 1/2 |
| -1 | 2/3 |
| 0 | 1 |
| +1 | 3/2 |
| +2 | 2 |
| +3 | 5/2 |
| +4 | 3 |
| +5 | 7/2 |
| +6 | 4 |

Further changes are capped at the stage limits. Stat stages are multiplicative rather than flat additions. A one-stage increase has a different proportional effect at different starting stages. Ordinary switching resets stages unless an explicit transfer effect preserves them.

Abilities can prevent, reverse, double, reflect, or react to stat changes. Unaware changes which opposing stages matter during a calculation; it does not remove the stages. Haze actually resets stages. A critical hit ignores particular unfavorable stages for its own damage calculation, not every statistic change on the field.

Champions uses its own stat-point calculation. Do not reconstruct a Pokémon using another game's EV/IV assumptions. The application should supply the appropriate actual statistics, including relevant Mega form statistics.

C11.text:
# Accuracy and evasion

Ordinary hit checks, accuracy and evasion stages, accuracy bypass, and special per-hit exceptions.

## Reference text

For an ordinary numeric-accuracy move, the user’s accuracy stage and the target’s evasion stage modify the hit check. The ordinary combined stage is accuracy minus evasion, limited to the range -6 to +6, subject to effects that ignore or modify either stage.

At combined stage `s`, the stage multiplier is `(3+s)/3` when `s` is nonnegative and `3/(3-s)` when `s` is negative. Thus +1 gives 4/3 and -1 gives 3/4. This is different from the ordinary stat-stage table.

Abilities, items, Gravity, weather, and move-specific rules can modify or bypass accuracy. Numeric 100% accuracy is not the same as bypassing accuracy checks: evasion or accuracy modifiers can still cause a normally 100%-accurate move to miss.

Bypassing accuracy does not automatically bypass a semi-invulnerable state, type immunity, protection, or a move's own failure condition. Multi-hit moves that perform additional accuracy checks need their particular per-hit rules. One-hit knockout moves also have their own accuracy and immunity rules.

C12.text:
# Ordinary damage

The inputs to ordinary damage, ordered modifiers, STAB, random variation, and special-stat exceptions.

## Reference text

For a standard damaging move, damage depends on level, effective base power, the relevant offensive and defensive statistics, and the applicable modifiers. Higher base power alone does not establish which attack will deal more damage or produce the best position.

The ordinary underlying relationship is proportional to `((2 × level / 5 + 2) × power × offense / defense) / 50 + 2`, followed by applicable modifiers. Showdown uses intermediate integer operations, ordered modifiers, and fixed-point rounding. This relationship explains the inputs; it is not an instruction to treat an approximate calculation as an exact damage roll.

Common modifiers include:

- **Same-type attack bonus:** normally 1.5× if the move shares one of the user's current applicable types. Sharing both types does not create two separate STAB multipliers. Abilities can alter STAB.
- **Type effectiveness:** the product of the applicable defensive matchups.
- **Spread damage:** normally 0.75× when the move qualifies as a spread hit.
- **Weather:** such as rain increasing Water damage and reducing Fire damage.
- **Critical hits:** normally 1.5×, with additional stage-handling rules.
- **Damage variation:** the ordinary random factor uses integers from 85 through 100 percent, inclusive.
- **Burn:** normally halves physical damage, with relevant exceptions.
- **Other effects:** screens, abilities, items, terrain, Helping Hand, and move-specific conditions.

Do not automatically apply this entire modifier chain to fixed-damage moves, HP-setting effects, one-hit knockout moves, indirect damage, or recoil. Their definitions specify different rules.

Physical and special describe the move's category, not necessarily the exact statistics it uses. Moves can explicitly use the target's Attack, the user's Defense, the target's physical Defense despite being special, or other substitutions. Use the supplied definition for those exceptions.

C13.text:
# Critical hits

Critical-hit chances, damage multiplier, ignored stages, screens, and effects critical hits do not bypass.

## Reference text

The normal critical-hit chance is 1/24. One additional critical-hit stage raises it to 1/8; two additional stages raise it to 1/2; three or more make a critical hit certain unless an effect prevents it. A move or ability can explicitly guarantee or prevent critical hits.

A critical hit normally multiplies damage by 1.5. It ignores negative stages in the offensive statistic used for that hit and positive stages in the defensive statistic used for that hit. Favorable offensive boosts and unfavorable defensive drops still matter.

A critical hit bypasses Reflect, Light Screen, and Aurora Veil's damage reduction. It does not generally bypass type immunities, Protect, Substitute, or every ability-based reduction. It does not automatically remove the burn damage penalty. Effects such as Sniper can alter the critical-hit damage multiplier.

C14.text:
# Damage, contact, and secondary effects

Distinct hit, damage, contact, stat-change, secondary-effect, and multi-hit triggers.

## Reference text

Contact-triggered effects depend on actual contact and the applicable ability/item rules. Rocky Helmet, Rough Skin, and protection variants can punish contact. A contact-preventing effect may alter those interactions without changing the move from physical to special or vice versa.

Taking damage, being hit, making contact, having a stat lowered, crossing an HP threshold, and being knocked out are different triggers. An effect tied to one of them should not be generalized to all the others.

A secondary effect is attempted only when its own conditions are reached. A knockout, Substitute, immunity, Shield Dust, Sheer Force, or another relevant effect can change whether the secondary effect occurs. Separate a move's secondary effect on the target from its guaranteed drawback on the user.

Multi-hit attacks can trigger effects between hits. A Substitute or Focus Sash can stop one hit without protecting against later hits. HP recovery or reactive effects can occur during the sequence. A move with two hits is not necessarily equivalent to one hit with twice its listed power.

C15.text:
# Statuses, volatile effects, and counters

Major status, volatile conditions, side and field effects, persistence, and differing counter meanings.

## Reference text

A Pokémon ordinarily has at most one major status: burn, poison, bad poison, paralysis, sleep, or freeze. Applying another normally does not replace an existing major status. Explicit moves such as Rest have their own replacement behavior.

Confusion, flinching, attraction, Taunt, Encore, Substitute, Leech Seed, and many other temporary effects are separate from major status and can coexist with it. Side conditions and field effects are separate again.

Major status usually persists through ordinary switching; many volatile effects do not. Switching does not automatically restore HP, PP, or a consumed item. An ability such as Natural Cure or Regenerator can add a specific switch-out benefit.

Counter meanings differ. Some effects count end-of-turn phases, some count attempted actions, some count successful uses, and some count hits taken. A Pokémon merely spending a turn on the bench does not necessarily advance its sleep or freeze counter. Use the supplied counter meaning and observed history.

Known duration, elapsed duration, and uncertain remaining duration are different facts. If a duration or hidden item has not been observed, do not turn a plausible duration into an exact remaining-turn count.

C16.text:
# Grounding and semi-invulnerability

Grounding, levitation, airborne effects, semi-invulnerability, and attacker versus recipient terrain checks.

## Reference text

Grounding determines exposure to many terrain benefits, terrain protections, entry hazards, Ground attacks, and trapping effects. It is not inferred from appearance.

Gravity, Ingrain, Smack Down, or an effective Iron Ball can ground a Pokémon. Otherwise, a current Flying type, an active applicable levitation ability such as Levitate or Eelevate, Magnet Rise, Telekinesis, or an effective Air Balloon can keep it ungrounded. Some moves or ability-negation effects override a particular immunity check.

Grounding can change during the turn. A type change, balloon being popped, ability suppression, or Gravity can therefore change whether a later effect works.

Semi-invulnerability is separate. A Pokémon using the hidden phase of Fly, Bounce, Dig, Dive, or Phantom Force is not simply “ungrounded.” Different attacks can reach different hidden states. A grounded Pokémon can still be temporarily unreachable by an ordinary attack. Apply the relevant move definition.

Terrain clauses specify whether they inspect the attacker or the recipient. For example, ordinary terrain type boosts inspect the grounded attacker, whereas Psychic Terrain's priority protection inspects the grounded target.

C17.text:
# Switching, pivots, and replacements

Voluntary switches, pivots, forced replacements, entry effects, resets, and eligible reserves.

## Reference text

A voluntary switch withdraws one active Pokémon and puts an eligible reserve in its position. The replacement can face attacks aimed at that position later in the turn. A switch is not an attack by the incoming Pokémon.

Ordinary switching clears stat stages and most volatile effects. It preserves current HP, PP, and major status unless a specific effect modifies them. Field weather, terrain, side conditions, and hazards remain unless another effect removes them.

Entry hazards and entry abilities can affect the incoming Pokémon before later actions occur. A Pokémon can faint on entry. The ordering of individual entry effects matters; do not assume every entry ability activates before every hazard or that all entry effects are simultaneous.

Pivot moves such as U-turn or Volt Switch attack first and can then request a replacement if their conditions succeed. Missing, protection, an immunity, the user fainting, or a competing switch-triggered effect can prevent the expected pivot. A damaging pivot's target changing or fainting is not the same as the user voluntarily switching before the attack.

Forced switches such as Roar and Dragon Tail have their own failure conditions and generally choose a reserve through the engine rather than letting the affected player freely choose. Baton Pass explicitly transfers certain effects that an ordinary switch clears.

A reserve must actually be available in the current battle. Team-preview Pokémon are not automatically all selected reserves. Both active Pokémon cannot switch into the same reserve simultaneously.

C18.text:
# Mega Evolution and current form

Mega eligibility, team resource, transformation timing, current form statistics and ability, and persistence.

## Reference text

Use the available Mega Evolution options supplied for the request. Only one Mega Evolution may be used by a side in a battle. Holding several compatible Mega Stones does not permit several Mega Evolutions.

A declaration is associated with the chosen action of an eligible active Pokémon. The transformation happens before ordinary moves and changes the Pokémon to its specified Mega form. Use that form's types, statistics, and ability for subsequent applicable events. The new Speed can affect the same turn's remaining action order.

Mega Evolution is not itself an extra damaging move. An entry-like effect from the new ability can occur during transformation. A Pokémon that already triggered a base-form ability on entry can therefore have a different ability after Mega Evolution.

Mega Evolution remains after switching out and fainting. The resulting form after Revival Blessing is uncertain. The Mega Stone is not consumed by the transformation.

The supplied form and eligibility fields determine the available transformation. A form whose name contains “Z” is not, for that reason, a Z-Move. Do not introduce Terastallization, Dynamax, or another generation's battle feature into this environment without an explicit supported action and rule.

C19.text:
# Abilities and held items

Ability suppression versus bypass, item presence versus consumption, and trigger-specific timing.

## Reference text

An ability can be known but currently ineffective because it is suppressed, bypassed for a particular interaction, or unavailable in the current form. These states are different. Neutralizing Gas suppresses applicable abilities while present; Mold Breaker-style effects bypass specified abilities during an applicable move without permanently deleting them.

Abilities can activate on entry, on a hit, when statistics change, at an HP threshold, on a knockout, on switching out, or during a residual phase. Merely naming the ability does not specify when it applies. Include its triggering condition and relevant exceptions.

A held item can be unknown, present and active, temporarily suppressed, consumed, removed, or replaced. An item that has been consumed does not activate again just because the Pokémon switches out. A suppression effect does not necessarily remove the item itself.

An item can be automatically consumed during another action; it does not require a separate chosen command. HP thresholds must be evaluated at the time specified by the item. Some items and abilities act between hits, while others act after an entire move.

Legality and item availability come from the selected Champions format. A familiar item from another VGC game must not be assumed available here. Current entity definitions and the request are the source of the Pokémon's item-related behavior.

C20.text:
# End-of-turn effects and fainting

Sequential residual events, effect expiry, fainting, replacement timing, and battle completion.

## Reference text

Residual effects execute in an order, rather than as one simultaneous sum of damage and healing. Early chip damage can cause a knockout before a later recovery effect. Expiration of weather, terrain, or another effect can change whether a later effect applies.

The relevant order includes weather processing; delayed attacks and Wish; terrain and selected recovery effects; Leech Seed; poison and burn; binding and Salt Cure; restrictions and delayed effects; Perish Song; expiration of side and field conditions; and later ability or item events. The library provides a more precise selected-effect ordering with explicit limits.

Fainted Pokémon cannot perform their pending ordinary actions. Knockouts can remove an ability's field influence or invalidate a partner interaction. Replacement requests follow the engine's timing; a knockout during a move does not always mean that a replacement immediately occupies the target's position before the rest of that move.

The engine determines battle completion and simultaneous-knockout resolution. Do not infer an exact winner from a simplified net-HP calculation when recoil, contact damage, delayed damage, or other queued events can change the result.

C21.text:
# Using the conditional library

When to load shared definitions, include dependencies, deduplicate rules, and preserve individual Pokémon state.

## Reference text

Apply a conditional entry only when its triggering effect is present or can arise from a considered action or opponent hypothesis. A reference to an ability or item does not assert that a particular Pokémon possesses it.

Include the full chain of needed definitions. Fake Out requires its own move data, priority, flinching, protection, and the relevant immunity rules. Psychic Terrain additionally requires grounding. A possible switch to a terrain-setting Pokémon can make that terrain relevant before it is on the field.

Use one shared definition per entity or mechanic. Per-Pokémon PP, current ability state, item state, counters, and restrictions remain attached to that individual Pokémon. Two Pokémon knowing Protect share the definition but do not share PP or consecutive-use counters.

This context provides rules and observed information for judgment. Exact damage outcomes, future opponent commands, and unrevealed random outcomes are not supplied unless explicitly identified as such in the current state. The selected action should remain a judgment under those information limits.

M01.text:
# Burn

Burn damage, physical-attack penalty, immunity, and relevant damage or ability exceptions.

## Reference text

Include when a considered Pokémon is burned or a considered effect can cause burn. Dependencies: major status, physical damage, residual order, relevant immunity and ability definitions.

Burn normally causes damage equal to 1/16 of the affected Pokémon's maximum HP at its burn residual event. The damage uses the engine's integer handling. Protect does not prevent this residual damage.

Burn normally halves damage from the Pokémon's physical attacks. It does not simply replace the Pokémon's displayed Attack statistic with half its value. Critical hits do not normally remove this penalty. Guts prevents this physical-damage penalty while providing its own status-dependent Attack increase. Facade has its specific exception to the penalty.

Fire types cannot ordinarily be newly burned. Abilities, terrain, existing major status, Substitute, or another relevant protection can prevent application. Acquiring a burn-immune type does not itself remove an existing burn. Magic Guard prevents ordinary burn chip damage but does not generally erase the burn's other consequences.

M02.text:
# Poison and bad poison

Poison and escalating bad poison, switch persistence and reset, immunity, healing, and damage prevention.

## Reference text

Include when poison, bad poison, Toxic, Toxic Spikes, or a poisoning secondary effect is relevant. Dependencies: major status, residual order, status immunity, hazard rules when applicable.

Ordinary poison deals 1/8 maximum HP at its poison residual event. Bad poison uses a counter: successive active poison events normally deal 1/16, 2/16, 3/16, and so forth, up to the engine's counter cap of 15. Round the base HP fraction before multiplying by the counter; rounding matters at HP thresholds.

Bad poison persists through ordinary switching, but its escalating counter resets for the next entry. Poison and bad poison are major statuses, so they normally cannot coexist with another major status. Poison and Steel types are immune to their initial application unless an applicable exception such as Corrosion overrides the type restriction.

Poison Heal changes ordinary poison damage into healing of 1/8 maximum HP at the relevant event. Magic Guard can prevent poison damage without curing the status. Do not infer that preventing one residual tick removes the underlying poison.

M03.text:
# Paralysis — Champions

Champions paralysis Speed reduction and action-failure probability, including Quick Feet interaction.

## Reference text

Include when paralysis exists or can be inflicted. Dependencies: Speed, action order, major status, Quick Feet if relevant.

Paralysis normally halves the Pokémon's Speed after the other applicable Speed modifiers, with integer truncation. An active Quick Feet ability prevents this halving and applies its own status-dependent Speed modifier.

When the before-move paralysis check is reached, there is a **1/8 probability, or 12.5%, that the Pokémon cannot execute its move**. Quick Feet does not remove that failure check. An earlier event that prevents execution can stop the action before this check is reached.

Electric types cannot ordinarily be newly paralyzed. Ground immunity to an Electric attack such as Thunder Wave is an additional move/type interaction, not general immunity to every possible source of paralysis. Ordinary switching does not cure paralysis.

M04.text:
# Sleep — Champions

Champions sleep counters, waking checks, Early Bird, Rest, bench time, and sleep prevention.

## Reference text

Include when sleep, Rest, Yawn, or a sleep-causing move is relevant. Dependencies: before-move checks, major status, sleep-prevention effects.

Ordinary sleep initializes a hidden counter to 2 with probability 1/3 and to 3 with probability 2/3. Each reached sleep check reduces the counter before deciding whether the Pokémon wakes. Without an intervening cure or modifier, the first sleep check prevents an ordinary move; the second check wakes the Pokémon in the 1/3 branch; otherwise the third check wakes it. The Pokémon can execute its chosen move on the check that wakes it.

These are sleep checks, not simply elapsed calendar turns. A Pokémon put to sleep before its action can reach its first sleep check in that same turn. Time spent on the bench does not itself consume these checks, and ordinary switching does not reset the remaining sleep counter in this environment.

Early Bird adds an extra counter decrement at each sleep check. Moves explicitly usable while asleep can still execute according to their definitions. Sleep Talk has its own selection and failure rules; knowing Sleep Talk does not make other selected moves sleep-usable.

Rest explicitly sets its own sleep counter to 3 after healing succeeds. Ordinarily, this prevents the next two ordinary move attempts and permits waking on the third. Do not use the ordinary random sleep distribution for Rest.

Sleep prevention can come from an ability or from grounded terrain effects. Electric Terrain does not wake a Pokémon that was already asleep. Sleep being prevented or cured may have different timing depending on the source.

M05.text:
# Freeze — Champions

Champions freeze checks, guaranteed expiry, thawing moves, typing, and effective sun.

## Reference text

Include when freeze exists or a considered effect can cause it. Dependencies: before-move checks, major status, thawing move flags and relevant immunities.

Ordinary freeze initializes a counter to 3. When its ordinary before-move check is reached, the counter decreases. If it has reached zero, the Pokémon thaws. Otherwise there is a **1/4 probability of thawing at that check**. A Pokémon that thaws can act on that action.

Without other effects, the first and second checks each offer a 25% thaw chance conditional on still being frozen; the third check guarantees thawing. This does not mean three guaranteed lost turns. Bench time does not itself perform a thaw check.

A move explicitly flagged to thaw its user can bypass the ordinary frozen-action block and clear freeze through its own execution. Certain hits can thaw the target. Ordinary damaging Fire moves can thaw a frozen target when the relevant damage event occurs; an immunity that prevents the hit can also prevent that cure. Use the move and ability definitions for exceptions.

Ice types cannot ordinarily be newly frozen. Effective sun prevents new freeze through its weather immunity rule; it is not a blanket instruction to clear every existing frozen status immediately. Freeze-Dry has **no freezing secondary effect in the pinned Champions data**.

M06.text:
# Confusion and flinching

Confusion counters and self-hits; flinch timing, prevention, and the distinction from attack damage.

## Reference text

Include when either effect exists or can be created. Dependencies: action order, volatile effects, Substitute and relevant prevention abilities.

Confusion is a volatile effect and can coexist with major status. Ordinary confusion initializes its counter uniformly to 2, 3, 4, or 5. Each reached confusion check first decrements that counter; reaching zero ends confusion before any self-hit roll. Consequently, without an intervening cure or modifier, there are one through four checks at which self-hitting is possible, followed by the check that ends confusion. Some sources, such as Axe Kick, have a different minimum initial counter.

At a reached check while still confused, the self-hit probability is **33/100**. A self-hit prevents the selected move. It uses the Pokémon's own Attack and Defense, including their stages, with a 40-power physical-like calculation and ordinary damage variation. This calculation does not run the ordinary damage-modifier chain: it has no ordinary type matchup, STAB, critical hit, screen reduction, or burn damage penalty. Ordinary switching removes confusion unless an explicit transfer effect carries it.

Flinching prevents the affected Pokémon's move when it reaches the flinch check in that turn. It does not remove an action already completed and does not normally carry into the next turn. An attacker moving after its target cannot retroactively cancel that target's completed move through flinching.

Inner Focus prevents flinching. Shield Dust can prevent a flinch that is a blocked secondary effect. Preventing the flinch does not necessarily prevent the attack's damage. Fake Out's damage and its flinch should therefore be considered separately.

M07.text:
# Yawn, attraction, and Perish Song

Delayed sleep, source-linked attraction, Perish Song counters, switching, and relevant prevention.

## Reference text

Include only the subrules relevant to considered effects. Dependencies: status prevention, volatile effects, switching, residual order, sound immunity for Perish Song.

Yawn creates a delayed sleep effect. It normally attempts to put the affected Pokémon to sleep at the end of the following turn if that Pokémon is still active and can then fall asleep. Ordinary switching clears the pending Yawn effect. Existing major status and sleep-prevention effects can prevent initial application or later sleep. Electric Terrain blocks Yawn for grounded Pokémon; Misty Terrain can allow the drowsy effect but prevents grounded Pokémon from actually falling asleep from it. Safeguard's initial-application and already-pending-Yawn behavior are different; see M24.

Attraction is a volatile source-linked effect, separate from major status. When it can be established under the move's gender and immunity conditions, a reached attraction check has a 50% chance to prevent the affected Pokémon's move. A genderless or same-gender pairing does not satisfy ordinary Attract's requirement. Leaving the field, losing the relevant source, or an explicit cure can end it. Include the precise source and prevention rule when this effect is used.

Perish Song assigns a perish counter to affected active Pokémon that do not already have one. The counter decreases at the end of the use turn and each subsequent turn: the displayed sequence proceeds through 3, 2, 1, and then 0, at which point the affected Pokémon faints. Ordinary switching removes the count; Baton Pass can transfer it. Protect and ordinary damage resistance do not turn Perish Song into an ordinary blocked attack. Soundproof can prevent the sound-based application. A Pokémon's existing perish counter is not simply refreshed by another use.

M08.text:
# Leech Seed, binding, Salt Cure, and Curse

Leech Seed, binding, Champions Salt Cure, and Curse: damage, source links, removal, and switching.

## Reference text

Include when an applicable persistent-damage effect exists or can be established. Dependencies: residual order, grounding and trapping as applicable, switching, Substitute, prevention abilities.

**Leech Seed:** At its residual event, the affected Pokémon normally loses 1/8 maximum HP and the Pokémon occupying the seeder's position receives the corresponding recovery, subject to damage and healing modifiers. Grass types are immune to its initial application. Ordinary switching by the seeded Pokémon removes it; the seeder's replacement can receive the healing. Baton Pass can carry the seeded effect. Rapid Spin or Mortal Spin can remove it under their own successful-use conditions.

**Binding moves:** Effects such as Wrap, Whirlpool, or Infestation normally restrict voluntary switching and cause 1/8 maximum-HP damage per applicable residual event for four or five turns. They normally end when the relevant source or target leaves. A binding effect is distinct from a trapping ability and from a move lock. Ghost-type trapping immunity and Champions Run Away can change the switch restriction without necessarily preventing the original hit or its damage-over-time effect. Substitute can remove the binding effect when successfully created. A repeated binding move does not ordinarily stack an independent second binding counter.

**Salt Cure — Champions:** The ongoing effect deals **1/16 maximum HP**, or **1/8** if the affected Pokémon currently has Water or Steel typing, at its residual event. Being both Water and Steel does not apply the enhanced rate twice. This is in addition to Salt Cure's initial attack. Ordinary switching removes the effect. Protect can block the initial eligible hit but does not stop residual damage from an already established effect.

**Curse:** Its effect depends on the user's current type. For a non-Ghost user, it lowers Speed one stage and raises Attack and Defense one stage. For a Ghost user, it normally sacrifices half the user's maximum HP and establishes a curse that removes one quarter of the target's maximum HP per residual event. The Ghost user's sacrifice can cause it to faint. Ordinary switching clears the target's curse, while Baton Pass can transfer it. Use the target and failure rules from the supplied move definition.

M09.text:
# Protect, Detect, and related personal protection

Protect-family scope, Champions PP, diminishing success, contact retaliation, and protection bypass versus removal.

## Reference text

Include when a relevant protection move is known or hypothesized. Dependencies: priority, move blockability, consecutive-use counter, bypass effects, residual damage.

Protect and Detect normally create personal protection for the remainder of the current turn, with priority +4. They block eligible moves from other Pokémon, including many damaging and status moves. They do not protect the partner automatically and do not stop already established residual effects such as burn, Leech Seed, or Salt Cure.

Success depends on the shared consecutive-protection counter. Starting fresh, the normal success probability is 1. After a success, the next relevant attempt is 1/3, then 1/9, 1/27, and so on, with the pinned counter capped at 729. A failure or a sufficient break in the chain resets the effect. Related protection moves can contribute to the same counter; switching from Protect to Detect does not provide a fresh guaranteed attempt. A protection move can also fail if no eligible action remains for it to precede.

In Champions, Protect's base PP is 5. That base value is not the current or maximum PP supplied for an individual Pokémon: the Champions PP transformation gives an ordinary base-5 move 8 maximum PP. Always use the request's per-Pokémon PP.

Personal protection variants have different scopes and punishments. King's Shield blocks damaging moves and can lower a contact attacker's Attack; it is not general protection against status moves. Spiky Shield can damage a contacting attacker. Baneful Bunker can poison one. Include the exact variant's retaliation condition, amount, and immunity checks when it appears.

Feint and particular other moves can break protection so later moves benefit. Merely bypassing protection for one hit is different from removing the protective effect for the rest of the turn. Use the supplied bypass or break behavior rather than assuming every exception is equivalent.

M10.text:
# Wide Guard and Quick Guard

Side protection against eligible spread or positive-priority moves, ally interactions, and shared protection counters.

## Reference text

Include when either guard is relevant. Dependencies: priority, target categories, protection bypass, shared protection counter.

Wide Guard has priority +3 and protects the user's side from eligible moves whose target category is all adjacent Pokémon or all adjacent foes. It can protect against an ally's spread move as well as an opponent's. It checks the category even when only one Pokémon is currently in reach. It does not generally block a single-target attack.

Quick Guard has priority +3 and protects the user's side from eligible moves with positive priority, including priority gained from an ability. It can block an eligible move from an ally. Acting early through an item or Speed alone is not equivalent to using a positive-priority move.

These guards do **not** make the ordinary consecutive-use failure roll themselves in this environment, so repeated uses are not subject to Protect's decreasing success chance. They can nevertheless update the shared counter that affects a subsequent personal-protection attempt. Other failure conditions, duplicate side protection, move bypass rules, and action timing still apply.

M11.text:
# Reflect, Light Screen, and Aurora Veil

Reflect, Light Screen, and Aurora Veil: doubles reduction, duration, setup conditions, bypass, and removal.

## Reference text

Include when a screen exists or can be set. Dependencies: move category, critical hits, screen removal, Infiltrator if relevant.

Reflect reduces eligible physical damage; Light Screen reduces eligible special damage. In doubles, the pinned engine uses a damage multiplier of **2732/4096**, approximately two thirds. This is a doubles-format reduction even when only one Pokémon remains active on that side, rather than a rule based solely on counting present partners.

Aurora Veil reduces eligible damage of both categories but requires effective snow when set. Once established, it does not require snow to remain in order to persist. Its reduction does not stack again with Reflect or Light Screen for the same attack.

These screens normally last five turns including the setup turn, or eight when the setter has an effective Light Clay. Critical hits and applicable Infiltrator attacks bypass their reduction. Brick Break and Psychic Fangs can remove relevant screens before their damage is calculated; Defog also has screen-removal behavior under its own rules.

Screens do not mean that all HP loss is reduced. Fixed damage, residual damage, costs, and special damage-setting effects require their own definitions.

M12.text:
# Substitute

Substitute HP cost, interception, status protection, bypass, multi-hit behavior, and switching or transfer.

## Reference text

Include when a Substitute exists or a considered Pokémon can create or transfer one. Dependencies: current HP, multi-hit attacks, sound and bypass tags, Infiltrator, residual effects.

Substitute costs one quarter of the user's maximum HP, rounded down, and creates a separate damage buffer with that HP. The move fails if a substitute already exists or the user cannot pay the required cost and remain alive. The substitute does not have a separate type chart; the protected Pokémon's relevant damage calculation still governs attacks against it.

An eligible attack damages the substitute instead of the Pokémon. Excess damage from the hit that breaks it does not overflow onto the Pokémon, but later hits of the same multi-hit attack can hit the Pokémon. Many opposing status effects and stat reductions are blocked while the substitute intercepts the move.

Moves with an applicable bypass property, including relevant sound moves, and attacks using Infiltrator can bypass it. Do not treat every field-wide or self-directed effect as a move aimed through the substitute. Existing weather/status/residual effects still affect the Pokémon according to their own rules.

Ordinary switching removes the substitute. Baton Pass can transfer it with its remaining HP. Successfully creating a substitute removes an ordinary binding volatile. Hitting a substitute is not necessarily the same as triggering an item that requires the holder itself to take damage.

M13.text:
# Redirection

Follow Me, Rage Powder, and ability-based redirection: valid targets, timing, powder immunity, and exceptions.

## Reference text

Include when Follow Me, Rage Powder, Lightning Rod, Storm Drain, or a redirection-bypassing effect is relevant. Dependencies: target eligibility, action order, powder immunity, ability suppression.

Follow Me and Rage Powder normally act at priority +2 and establish redirection for the remainder of the turn. Suitable opposing single-target moves are redirected to the user while it is a valid target. They do not generally redirect an entire spread move, a self-targeted move, or a field effect.

Redirection begins only after the redirecting effect is established. Fake Out at +3 can act before a normally ordered Follow Me or Rage Powder. A redirector that faints or becomes an invalid target cannot simply continue drawing every later attack.

Rage Powder additionally depends on whether the attacker is affected by powder. A Grass-type attacker or one protected by an applicable powder-immunity ability can ignore Rage Powder. Follow Me does not share this powder limitation.

Lightning Rod draws eligible single-target Electric moves to its holder and Storm Drain does the same for Water moves. They can interact with moves from either side; deliberately targeting an ally can therefore matter. Their type immunity and Special Attack increase are separate from whether redirection was needed.

Follow Me/Rage Powder have precedence over those ability-based redirection effects when their conditions are met. Competing ability redirectors use their specific ordering rules; the fastest applicable holder normally wins, with ability activation order relevant to the documented tie case. Snipe Shot and other explicit bypass effects need their own exception entries.

M14.text:
# Helping Hand and ally interaction

Helping Hand, beneficial or harmful ally attacks, Telepathy, Friend Guard, and Ally Switch.

## Reference text

Include when ally support, an ally-targeted attack, or ally damage is relevant. Dependencies: targeting, move timing, relevant ability and protection rules.

Helping Hand normally has priority +5 and multiplies the power of the partner's applicable attack that turn by 1.5. It fails if there is no eligible partner or the partner has already moved. It does not grant the partner another action. The partner still needs to execute an attack that can benefit, reach its target, and pass the relevant checks.

A support move can affect both sides' Pokémon if its targeting permits that. An ally-targeted damaging move can activate an immunity ability or another beneficial reaction, but it can also cause genuine damage or trigger harmful effects. Do not assume “ally” automatically makes an attack harmless.

Telepathy prevents damage from an ally's damaging attacks when effective. Friend Guard reduces eligible damage received by the holder's allies to 3/4; it does not provide that reduction to the holder itself. Each ability's suppression and bypass rules still apply.

Ally Switch swaps the two allied active positions without switching either Pokémon to the bench. It does not reset ordinary switch-out counters or activate ordinary entry abilities. Repeated use has its own diminishing success mechanic and should not be treated as indefinitely guaranteed.

M15.text:
# Weather

Rain, sun, sandstorm, and snow: duration, damage and defensive modifiers, move effects, and suppression.

## Reference text

Include when weather is active or a considered move, switch-in ability, or Mega ability can set it. Dependencies: duration, suppression, relevant move/ability definitions, residual order.

Only one ordinary weather is active at a time. Establishing a different weather replaces the previous one. Ordinary rain, sun, sandstorm, and snow normally last five turns, or eight when established by a Pokémon with the corresponding effective weather-extending rock. The creation turn counts toward the duration. An ability-created ordinary weather is not automatically permanent.

| Weather | General effects |
| --- | --- |
| Rain | Water damage is ordinarily multiplied by 1.5 and Fire damage by 0.5. |
| Sun | Fire damage is ordinarily multiplied by 1.5 and Water damage by 0.5; new freeze is normally prevented. |
| Sandstorm | Rock types receive 1.5× Special Defense. Susceptible active Pokémon take 1/16 maximum-HP sand damage at the relevant weather event. Rock, Ground, and Steel types are naturally immune to that chip damage. |
| Snow | Ice types receive 1.5× Defense. Snow itself does not inflict hail-style chip damage. |

These boosts are not generic same-type attack boosts: sandstorm does not by itself boost all Rock attacks, and snow does not by itself boost all Ice attacks.

Move-specific weather behavior matters. Thunder and Hurricane bypass their ordinary accuracy checks in rain and ordinarily have 50% accuracy in sun. Blizzard bypasses its ordinary accuracy check in snow. Solar Beam and Solar Blade ordinarily skip their charging turn in sun and have reduced power in certain other weather. Weather Ball changes type and power with applicable weather. The relevant move definitions must accompany those interactions.

Swift Swim, Chlorophyll, Sand Rush, and Slush Rush provide their own weather-dependent Speed effects when the matching ability is present and active. A species does not receive such an effect merely because it is associated with rain, sun, sand, or snow.

Cloud Nine and Air Lock suppress the effects of weather while active. Suppression does not necessarily delete the stored weather or stop its duration from elapsing. When suppression ends, the remaining weather can matter again. The order of competing weather setters determines the resulting weather.

M16.text:
# Terrain framework

Terrain replacement, duration, grounding, side-independent effects, and identifying whose grounding matters.

## Reference text

Include with any terrain entry. Dependencies: grounding, duration, active ability/item state.

One terrain can be active at a time, independently of weather. A new different terrain replaces the previous terrain. Terrain normally lasts five turns including its setup turn, or eight if the setter has an effective Terrain Extender.

Many terrain effects require grounding, but they do not all test the same Pokémon. Type boosts ordinarily test the attacking Pokémon; priority protection and status prevention test the affected target. Terrain does not automatically change a Pokémon's type.

A Pokémon becoming grounded or ungrounded during the turn can gain or lose a terrain interaction. A terrain-setting switch or Mega Evolution can establish terrain before ordinary attacks. Terrain does not protect only the side that created it.

M17.text:
# Electric Terrain

Grounded Electric attack boost, sleep prevention, Yawn interaction, and existing sleep.

## Reference text

Dependencies: M16, grounding, sleep and Yawn.

Electric attacks by grounded Pokémon have their power multiplied by 1.3. Grounded Pokémon cannot newly fall asleep, including through Rest, while the prevention applies. Already sleeping Pokémon are not automatically awakened.

Grounded Pokémon cannot acquire Yawn's delayed effect or fall asleep from an existing Yawn effect while the relevant Electric Terrain protection applies. A Flying or otherwise ungrounded Pokémon does not automatically receive this sleep protection.

M18.text:
# Grassy Terrain

Grounded Grass power, residual healing, selected Ground-move reduction, and Grassy Glide priority.

## Reference text

Dependencies: M16, grounding, residual healing, relevant move definitions.

Grass attacks by grounded Pokémon have their power multiplied by 1.3. Grounded active Pokémon recover 1/16 maximum HP at the terrain's recovery event, including the relevant final-turn recovery before the terrain expires.

Earthquake, Bulldoze, and Magnitude have their power halved against grounded targets while the terrain applies. This is not a blanket halving of every Ground move.

Grassy Glide gains one priority level when its user is grounded and Grassy Terrain applies. Use that resulting priority when considering action order and priority-blocking effects.

M19.text:
# Misty Terrain

Grounded status and confusion prevention, Dragon power reduction, and delayed Yawn sleep.

## Reference text

Dependencies: M16, grounding, major status, confusion and Yawn.

Grounded Pokémon are protected from newly inflicted major status and confusion. Existing statuses are not automatically cured. Grounded recipients take half the ordinary power from Dragon attacks under the terrain's rule, regardless of whether the Dragon attacker is grounded.

Misty Terrain does not provide a general Fairy attack boost. A grounded Pokémon can become drowsy from Yawn, but the terrain prevents the resulting sleep while its protection applies. If the protection disappears before the sleep event, the remaining Yawn conditions must be considered again.

M20.text:
# Psychic Terrain

Grounded Psychic power, opposing priority protection, ally exceptions, and Expanding Force changes.

## Reference text

Dependencies: M16, grounding, priority, targeting.

Psychic attacks by grounded Pokémon have their power multiplied by 1.3. Grounded targets are protected from opposing moves with priority greater than zero when those moves attempt to affect them.

The target's grounding matters for this protection. An airborne attacker does not bypass it merely by being airborne, and an airborne target is not protected merely because its partner is grounded. Ally-directed moves are exempt from this opposing-move protection; Psychic Terrain does not block Helping Hand merely for having positive priority.

Expanding Force gains its special power increase and all-foes targeting when its user is grounded in Psychic Terrain. That change can make spread-damage and Wide Guard rules relevant. A grounded-target priority block is different from the broad side protection supplied by Armor Tail.

M21.text:
# Gravity, Trick Room, Tailwind, and other rooms

Gravity, Trick Room, Tailwind, Wonder Room, and Magic Room: duration, ordering, grounding, and suppression.

## Reference text

Include the specific effects present or producible. Dependencies: Speed, grounding, accuracy, duration.

**Gravity:** Normally lasts five turns. It grounds applicable Pokémon and increases ordinary move accuracy by a factor of 5/3 through the accuracy system. It prevents specified airborne moves and ends certain airborne states. It does not remove every unrelated immunity or protection. The exact list of gravity-blocked moves must come from the considered move definitions.

**Trick Room:** Normally lasts five turns including its setup turn. It reverses the effective-Speed comparison within each priority bracket. Using it again while active ends the effect. Its own ordinary priority is -7. Champions uses a straightforward reversed Speed comparison rather than the old extreme-Speed wraparound.

**Tailwind:** Doubles the Speed of Pokémon on the user's side for four turns including setup. The effect belongs to the side and persists if the setter switches or faints. It can change the order of actions remaining in the current turn. Under Trick Room, becoming faster can make a Pokémon move later within its priority bracket.

**Wonder Room:** Temporarily exchanges the defensive-stat roles specified by its implementation for five turns. It does not simply exchange the displayed Defense and Special Defense stage counters. Use the supplied effective defensive information for unusual stat-substitution attacks. A second use ends it.

**Magic Room:** Normally suppresses the ordinary effects of held items for five turns. Suppression is not consumption or removal. Item-dependent form changes have special handling. A second use ends it. The presence of a held item alone is therefore insufficient to assume that its ordinary battle effect currently applies.

M22.text:
# Taunt, Encore, Disable, Torment, and Imprison

Taunt, Encore, Disable, Torment, and Imprison, including selected-action changes and Champions exceptions.

## Reference text

Include each relevant restriction. Dependencies: last move, PP, current actions, status-versus-damaging category, relevant immunity and cure definitions.

**Taunt:** Prevents ordinary status moves for the target's next three relevant turns. It can prevent a previously selected status move if Taunt takes effect before that move executes. Oblivious, Aroma Veil, a timely Mental Herb, or another applicable effect can change the result.

**Encore:** Normally forces repetition of the target's last eligible move for its next three turns. It fails without an eligible previous move or when the relevant PP/eligibility conditions are not met, and ends when the encored move runs out of PP. It can replace a move already selected but not yet executed. Encore adjusts the pending action for the repeated move's priority. Mental Herb’s effect on that pending priority is uncertain.

**Disable:** Normally disables the target's last eligible move for four turns. A move already selected can be prevented when its Disable check is reached. Its Champions before-move logic has a special exception for moves marked as unable to be used twice consecutively; the server's request and exact move rules must govern that edge case.

**Torment:** Prevents ordinary selection of the same move on successive turns while active. It does not mean the Pokémon forgets that move or loses its remaining PP.

**Imprison:** While its user remains active, opponents cannot use moves that the user also knows. The effect depends on the user's current known moves and continued presence, not on which one of those moves it selected this turn.

Restrictions can combine. A single available move can become unusable, leading to Struggle or another forced action supplied by the engine. Legal options at request time still need to be distinguished from successful execution after a faster opponent changes the state.

M23.text:
# Choice lock, charging, recharge, and first-turn moves

Choice lock, charging, recharge, first-action moves, entry history, and forced Struggle.

## Reference text

Include the relevant mechanics. Dependencies: PP, action history, switching, move definition.

Choice Scarf multiplies Speed by 1.5 while effective and normally locks the holder into the first move it executes. Ordinary switching clears the move lock. Temporary item suppression and changes to the held item can affect the lock's operation. A Choice item being familiar from another game does not make that item legal in this regulation; this entry uses Choice Scarf because it is present in the pinned Champions item data.

A two-turn move can spend one action charging or entering a semi-invulnerable state and perform its attack on the following action. The continuation, target, and escape rules are move-specific. Do not treat the second turn as an unrestricted fresh choice. Solar Beam under sun is an example of a condition that can remove a charging turn.

Recharge moves can force a following action to be spent recharging when their triggering conditions are met. A forced recharge is distinct from paralysis, and the request can already encode the forced action. Multi-turn rampage moves have their own locking duration and aftermath.

Fake Out and First Impression are available only for the qualifying first move action after entry. The Champions override disables them once that entry's action opportunity has been used; an earlier action prevented by a status does not necessarily preserve the opportunity. Ordinary switching out and back in resets the relevant entry state. Fake Out has priority +3 and a flinching secondary effect; First Impression has priority +2 and base power 100 in Champions.

If no ordinary known move can be selected, the engine can supply Struggle. Struggle deals typeless damage to a selected-by-engine opposing target and has its own quarter-maximum-HP recoil rule. It is not a new move that can be chosen freely when other moves remain available.

M24.text:
# Safeguard, healing, and healing prevention

Safeguard, Wish, Roost, weather-dependent healing, Pain Split, and healing prevention.

## Reference text

Include the subrules relevant to current or considered effects. Dependencies: major status, residual order, source/recipient identity, items and abilities.

Safeguard normally protects the user's side from opposing applications of major status and confusion for five turns. It does not cure an existing condition. Its Yawn rule prevents initial application but does not necessarily stop an already pending Yawn from causing sleep. Infiltrator and explicit bypass effects need their own handling.

Recovery cannot ordinarily raise HP above maximum HP. A healing move can fail at full HP or be prevented by a healing-block effect. Different recovery moves restore different fractions and may use different integer rounding; use their specific definitions at exact HP thresholds.

Wish establishes a delayed recovery attached to a position. At the end of the following turn, the occupant of that position can recover half the original user's maximum HP, rounded down. Switching the Wish user can therefore deliver the recovery to a reserve. The recipient's own maximum HP is not used to set Wish's healing amount.

Roost ordinarily restores half maximum HP and removes the user's Flying typing for the remainder of the turn if the healing succeeds. A pure Flying user temporarily becomes Normal under the move's rule. This can change a later Ground matchup and terrain exposure; it does not permanently change the species.

Synthesis, Morning Sun, and Moonlight ordinarily recover one half maximum HP without weather, two thirds in effective sun, and one quarter in rain, sandstorm, or snow, subject to their precise definitions.

Pain Split sets both Pokémon toward the rounded average of their current HP, capped separately by each Pokémon's maximum HP. It is not an ordinary damaging attack followed by an ordinary healing move.

Psychic Noise can impose a two-turn healing-block effect through its secondary-effect handling. That condition can prevent healing and draining moves and many ability/item recovery effects while the target remains active. Pain Split and Regenerator are exempt from this healing block.

M25.text:
# Entry hazards and hazard removal

Entry hazards, layers, grounding, typing, prevention, absorption, and distinct removal methods.

## Reference text

Include when hazards are present or a considered move can set them. Dependencies: switching, grounding, type effectiveness, status/stat-change prevention.

Hazards belong to a side and affect eligible Pokémon entering that side. Setting a hazard does not itself apply all its entry consequences to Pokémon already standing there. Ordinary switching does not remove hazards.

| Hazard | Ordinary entry effect |
| --- | --- |
| Stealth Rock | Loses 1/8 maximum HP multiplied by Rock effectiveness: commonly 1/32, 1/16, 1/8, 1/4, or 1/2. It is not restricted to grounded Pokémon. |
| Spikes | Grounded entrants lose 1/8, 1/6, or 1/4 maximum HP for one, two, or three layers. |
| Toxic Spikes | Eligible grounded entrants are poisoned at one layer or badly poisoned at two. A grounded Poison-type entrant can absorb the layers. Steel immunity prevents poisoning but does not itself absorb the layers. |
| Sticky Web | Lowers the grounded entrant's Speed by one stage, subject to applicable prevention, reversal, and reaction effects. |

The currently effective ability, item, grounding state, and status immunity can change hazard consequences. A Pokémon may faint from entry damage before a later event benefits it.

Removal moves differ. Rapid Spin and Mortal Spin require their own successful interaction and remove specified effects from the user's side. Defog can remove hazards and other field/side effects under its broader rules. Tidy Up removes its specified hazards and substitutes. Do not treat these moves as interchangeable generic “clear all effects” actions.

When multiple hazards coexist, their application order can affect HP thresholds and reactions. The exact order for every combination is unspecified; do not assume a universal sequence.

M26.text:
# Ability interactions

Ability-effect families, triggers, prevention, suppression, bypass, and changed abilities; exact entity exceptions still needed.

## Reference text

Include only entries matching a known ability or explicit ability hypothesis, together with the underlying mechanic. These summaries describe common interactions; an entity's complete resolved definition remains necessary for its unusual exceptions.

| Ability or family | Decision-relevant rule |
| --- | --- |
| Intimidate | On entry, attempts to lower opposing active Pokémon's Attack by one stage. Substitute, prevention abilities, and specific Intimidate immunities can block it. |
| Inner Focus | Prevents flinching and the ordinary Intimidate Attack reduction while effective. It does not make an incoming Fake Out deal zero damage. |
| Clear Body / Hyper Cutter | Clear Body prevents externally caused stat-stage reductions; Hyper Cutter protects Attack specifically. Self-inflicted drops are a different case. |
| Defiant / Competitive | React to applicable stat reductions caused by an opponent with +2 Attack or +2 Special Attack, respectively. Do not assume a partner's reduction triggers them. |
| Contrary / Simple | Contrary reverses stage-change directions. Simple doubles the stage-change amount. Stage caps still apply. |
| Unaware | Ignores specified opposing offensive/accuracy stages when defending and defensive/evasion stages when attacking. It does not erase those stages or ignore every item, ability, weather effect, or burn penalty. |
| Prankster | Adds +1 priority to status moves. Applicable opposing Dark targets are immune; self/ally support and field effects need their own targeting interpretation. |
| Armor Tail / Dazzling / Queenly Majesty | Prevent eligible opposing positive-priority moves from affecting the holder or its allies. They do not require their protected recipients to be grounded. |
| Levitate / Eelevate | Provide the applicable Ground and grounding-related immunities while effective. Eelevate also has a knockout-triggered stat increase; that extra rule must be supplied if the ability is present. |
| Lightning Rod / Storm Drain | Provide the relevant Electric/Water immunity, redirection, and +1 Special Attack reaction. See M13. |
| Water Absorb / Volt Absorb / Earth Eater | An applicable Water/Electric/Ground move is negated and can restore one quarter maximum HP. Full HP does not turn the immunity off. |
| Sap Sipper | Negates applicable Grass moves and can raise Attack one stage. |
| Flash Fire | Negates applicable Fire moves and establishes its Fire-offense boost after activation. Blocking a Fire hit can also prevent it from thawing the holder. |
| Guts / Quick Feet | Status-dependent Attack or Speed boosts, with their respective burn/paralysis modifier exceptions. They do not cure the status. |
| Natural Cure / Regenerator | On ordinary eligible switch-out, cure major status or recover one third maximum HP, respectively. Champions explicitly reports these effects in its protocol. |
| Run Away — Champions | Removes the ordinary trapping restriction through its trapping hooks. It does not imply unrestricted choice during every recharge or move lock. |
| Healer — Champions | At its residual opportunity, independently has a 50% chance to cure an adjacent ally's existing major status. It does not cure the holder through this ally effect. |
| Sturdy | At full HP, survives an otherwise lethal eligible hit with 1 HP; blocks one-hit knockout moves. A later hit can still knock it out. |
| Multiscale | Halves eligible attack damage while the holder is at full HP. Entry damage can remove that condition before an attack. |
| Rough Skin / Iron Barbs | An applicable contact attacker loses one eighth of its own maximum HP. |
| Magic Guard | Prevents many indirect damage sources, without eliminating status, move restrictions, HP costs, confusion self-damage, or every recoil-like effect. |
| Shield Dust | Prevents applicable secondary effects from other Pokémon's attacks. An effect can be secondary even with a 100% listed chance. |
| Sheer Force | Boosts qualifying attacks by 1.3 and removes their qualifying secondary effects. It also suppresses specified after-move reactions; do not infer the full reaction list from the power boost alone. |
| Serene Grace | Increases qualifying secondary-effect chances under its rules; it does not guarantee that the primary hit succeeds. |
| Skill Link | Makes qualifying variable-hit moves use their maximum hit count and changes certain per-hit accuracy handling. |
| Soundproof / Bulletproof / Overcoat | Prevent their specified sound, bullet, or powder/weather interactions. A visual animation is not evidence that a move has a particular tag. |
| Insomnia / Sweet Veil | Prevent relevant sleep. Insomnia can cure its holder on gaining the ability; Sweet Veil's protection does not immediately wake already sleeping allies. |
| Purifying Salt | Prevents major status and Yawn and reduces incoming Ghost attack damage through its offensive-stat modifier. |
| Battle Armor / Shell Armor | Prevent critical hits while effective. |
| Pressure | Can increase opposing PP expenditure for applicable targeted moves. It does not simply double every opposing move's PP cost regardless of target. |
| Unnerve | Prevents opposing ordinary berry consumption while active. It does not delete the berry. |
| Scrappy | Allows applicable Normal and Fighting moves to affect Ghost targets and provides its Intimidate immunity. Other immunities and protections can still apply. |

Ability negation deserves its own distinction. **Mold Breaker-style bypass** applies to an enumerated set of abilities for relevant move interactions. **Neutralizing Gas** suppresses applicable other abilities while its active conditions hold. **Gastro Acid**, **Skill Swap**, and **Entrainment** have distinct suppression or replacement rules and lists of abilities that cannot be affected. Never turn any of these into “all abilities are always ignored.”

An ability can change during Mega Evolution, copying, swapping, suppression ending, or a form transition. Entry-like triggers on gaining an ability can therefore matter in the middle of a turn. Preserve current ability state and activation history where known.

M27.text:
# Held-item interactions

Common held-item effects, consumption, thresholds, suppression, compatible Mega Stones, and triggered switches.

## Reference text

Include only the actual or explicitly hypothesized item entries. Dependencies: item presence and suppression, contact, damage timing, threshold checks, corresponding field effects.

| Item | Relevant behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Focus Sash | Consumed to preserve 1 HP against an eligible otherwise lethal hit when the holder begins that hit at full HP. Earlier chip damage or a later hit can defeat the protection. |
| Focus Band | Has a 10% chance to preserve 1 HP against an eligible otherwise lethal attack; it is different from Focus Sash's full-HP condition and consumption. |
| Sitrus Berry | Normally consumed when HP is at or below half maximum HP, restoring one quarter maximum HP if consumption and healing are permitted. |
| Lum Berry | Can be consumed to cure major status or confusion. It is not an ongoing immunity after consumption. |
| Mental Herb | A one-use cure for specified mental/move restrictions including attraction, Taunt, Encore, Disable, Torment, and the relevant healing-block condition. |
| White Herb | A one-use reset of negative stat stages to zero when its condition is reached; positive stages remain. |
| Rocky Helmet | Punishes applicable contact with damage equal to one sixth of the attacker's maximum HP. |
